Duane’s syndrome, November 2025

# **Duane’s syndrome**

## **This leaflet explains the eye condition known as Duane’s syndrome, how the condition effects eye movement and what management options are available, if required.**

## **What is Duane’s syndrome?**

### Duane’s syndrome is a horizontal eye movement difference, which is present from birth but is often not noticed until the child is older. Duane’s syndrome can affect either eye or both eyes.

## **What causes Duane’s syndrome?**

### In Duane’s syndrome there is mis-wiring of the nerves to the eye muscles. This means the eye muscles do not receive the correct signals, making it harder for the eyes to move in certain directions – in this case, side to side.

## **Other features of Duane’s syndrome include:**

### • Changes to the eyelids when looking side to side. • People with Duane’s often move their head to look to the side rather than just use their eyes alone.

### • Head posture change, where the head can be seen to turn towards the affected side.

### • Strabismus (turn in the eye or squint) and a need for glasses.

## **What is the treatment for Duane’s syndrome?**

### Children with Duane’s syndrome are regularly monitored up until the age of 7 but generally, they do not need treatment. Children often have a slight change to their head posture to compensate for their eye muscle restriction which typically remains present into adulthood.

### • If your child has a change to their head posture, **do not** correct this, as correction can cause visual symptoms such as double vision and difficulty for your child to use their eyes together as a pair, causing visual discomfort.

# Guidelines for the Management of Strabismus in Childhood

* 16 Mar 2012
* RCOphth

[Download](https://www.rcophth.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/2012-SCI-250-Guidelines-for-Management-of-Strabismus-in-Childhood-2012.pdf)

This guideline is designed for ophthalmologists managing children with strabismus (syn.squint), which is defined as a pathological misalignment of the visual axes. This is a broad subject and the reader is referred to comprehensive texts, for further information see bibliography (page 42).

The guidelines are intended to give general principles of management. It is assumed throughout this document that professionals dealing with common and uncommon cases of strabismus will have had adequate training and experience to manage children with these conditions. This document represents the current view of best practice endorsed by the College. Please also refer to the Royal College Quality standards document and Ophthalmic services for children. The management of strabismus in childhood is multidisciplinary matter and usually involves parents and children, ophthalmologists, orthoptists and optometrists.

General practitioners, health visitors, paediatricians and paediatric neurologists may also become involved in the management of children with strabismus. It is desirable that these parties are committed to locally agreed care pathways, covering visual screening, referral, assessment, treatment and the monitoring of progress of children identified with strabismus. The latter is particularly important, as it is common that information will change with development, and multiple follow up visits will be required. Written information about strabismus should be available. Adequate time should be made available by the clinicians involved, in order to explain the terminology, the possible treatments, what they involve and for the consenting procedures that are required for surgical intervention.

### **What is Duane’s syndrome? (also known as Duane’s Retraction syndrome)** This is a congenital (meaning present from birth) eye movement condition which can affect one or both eyes. The left eye is most commonly affected and females are more commonly affected than males. **You will notice:**

###  Restricted movement of one (unilateral Duane’s syndrome) or both eyes (bilateral

### Duane’s syndrome) usually when looking from side to side (horizontal eye movements).

###  Changes to the eyelids when looking from side to side: the affected eye lids often widen

...

###  There may or may not be a squint present in the straight ahead position.  Vision may be reduced in one eye

### **What causes Duane’s syndrome?** It is generally thought that the most likely cause of Duane’s syndrome, is a “mis-wiring” of the nerves which control eye movement. This means that the eye muscles don’t receive the correct signals to move the eyes from side to side. Alternatively it may be caused by a problem with the eye muscles, which may be thin or tight and less elastic than usual. **Is there any treatment for Duane’s syndrome?** Most children with Duane’s syndrome will be observed in the Orthoptic department for a period of time, to ensure their vision develops properly in each eye. #### New-onset squint with ataxia, vomiting or headache

##### 1\.30.2

Refer immediately children with new-onset squint that occurs together with ataxia, vomiting or headache to acute paediatric services.

#### Paralytic squint

##### 1\.30.3

[Refer urgently](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng127/chapter/terms-used-in-this-guideline) children with paralytic squint for neurological assessment, even in the absence of other signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure.

#### Non-paralytic squint

##### 1\.30.4

[Refer](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng127/chapter/terms-used-in-this-guideline) children with non-paralytic squint to ophthalmology services.

Why the committee made the recommendations

The committee used their knowledge and experience, together with validation by external experts, to develop the recommendations on squint.

###### New-onset squint with loss of fundal ('red') reflex

The committee agreed that referral should be immediate as new-onset squint with loss of fundal ('red') reflex in 1 or both eyes can indicate a retinoblastoma, or other progressive pathology of the eye. Additionally, following post publication feedback, NICE felt it was important to highlight that a new-onset squint with loss of

...

may also indicate a neurological condition associated with raised intracranial pressure or a brain tumour.

###### New-onset squint with ataxia, vomiting or headache

New-onset squint presenting with accompanying symptoms such as ataxia, vomiting or headache can indicate raised intracranial pressure. The committee agreed that children presenting with squint and any of these symptoms should be referred immediately.

###### Paralytic squint

Intracerebral tumour or inflammation can present with restriction of movement of 1 or both eyes, so the committee agreed that this symptom should trigger urgent referral.

###### Non-paralytic squint

In a non-paralytic squint, the child retains the ability to move both eyes fully in all directions.

## What is Duane`s Retraction Syndrome?

Duane’s Retraction Syndrome is a type of eye movement disorder that can affect one or both eyes when looking to the right and/or left hand side. It is commonly seen to affect the left eye and occurs more often in females than males. It can also be associated with a turn in either eye in the straight ahead position known as a squint (strabismus). It is most frequently present at birth but may not be seen until a little later in childhood when a child becomes more interested in objects around them.

The diagram below shows what may be seen in an individual with a type of Left Duane’s syndrome:

## What is the cause of Duane`s Retraction Syndrome?

There are six muscles around each eye controlled by three nerves which are responsible for moving the eyes in different directions. The muscles work in pairs, for the eye to move one must contract whilst its paired muscle relaxes.

There are a number of theories as to the cause of Duane’s Retraction Syndrome. The most notable theory is that there is a ‘miss-wiring

...

Other theories suggest a thin, tight or inelastic eye muscle is responsible for Duane’s Retraction Syndrome.

## Can this impact vision and why do I need to attend appointments?

Duane’s Retraction Syndrome does not affect the vision directly and, in most cases, people will use both eyes together normally.

...

However, there could be an associated squint or need for glasses. In some cases, an individual with Duane’s Retraction Syndrome may adopt a very subtle head posture to make it more comfortable.

...

For most people, Duane’s Retraction Syndrome does not cause significant problems with vision and is not usually noticeable to others. Treatment is generally not required unless there is an associated squint or a need to wear glasses. Surgery may be considered if the squint is large and/or the head posture used to compensate is large and/or uncomfortable. This would only be in marked cases and would need to be discussed with your ophthalmologist (eye doctor).

## Paediatric information: 8-12 year olds

# **Duane** **’s Retraction S** **yndrome**

### Duane’s syndrome is when one (or sometimes both) eyes don’t turn to the side very well and the eyelids open and close as the eyes try to turn. Usually, it’s difficult for the eye to look towards the side, away from the nose. Sometimes, it also cannot look towards the nose. **What causes it?** There are six muscles on the outside of each eyeball which move the eyes around. To move the eyes, the brain sends messages through nerves to the muscles. In people with Duane’s syndrome, the nerves get connected wrongly so the messages from the brain go to the wrong muscles. **How the world looks to you** Most people with Duane’s syndrome can see very well. **How you look to the world** When you look straight ahead, usually no one can tell you have Duane’s syndrome. People may notice that your eyes don’t move around properly, or that your eyes don’t point straight some of the time, and you may look as if you’re winking when you’re not.

### **How can the doctor tell?** The orthoptist and the doctor will be able to tell you have Duane’s syndrome simply by watching how your eyes move around. **Getting it sorted** You will need to come to the eye clinic from time to time to check you have good vision. Sometimes, we give you glasses or, in young children, an eyepatch for a few hours a day, to help you see well. Usually no other treatment is needed. If the Duane’s syndrome causes a lot of problems, like having to turn your head a lot, or if you have a noticeable squint even looking straight ahead, doctors can do an operation to make this better, but they cannot make your eye movements normal, even with an operation.

# **Duane** **’s Retraction S** **yndrome**

### Duane’s syndrome is a rare eye condition where one or sometimes both eyes do not move to the left or right fully and the eyelids may open and close as the eyes try to turn. In rare forms of Duane’s syndrome there can also be other problems, for example with the person’s hands. **What causes it?** There are six muscles on the outside of each eyeball which allow us to turn the eye in all the directions we want to look. To move the eyes, the brain sends electrical signals along nerve fibres to the muscles. These nerve fibres and muscles develop before we are born. Duane syndrome is caused by a ‘miswiring’ of the nerves and eye muscles. Nerve fibres that should have connected to one muscle do not develop properly, causing that muscle not to work so the eye cannot move in one direction. Nerve fibres become connected to the wrong muscle so that the eye may get pulled backwards into the socket which makes the eyelids look as if they are closing and opening, or it will cause the eye to shoot up and down, when it turns in and out.

### **How the world looks to you** For most people, Duane’s syndrome does not cause any problem with vision. In some cases, people may notice double vision some of the time or, rarely, most or all of the time. **How you look to the world** The condition is usually not noticeable when you look straight ahead. Other people might notice that one eye does not move to one side, that you have a squint (the eyes do not point straight) some of the time, or that you look like you’re winking when you look in some directions. Some people with Duane’s may turn their head to the side to see better. **How can the doctor tell?** The orthoptist and the doctor will be able to diagnose Duane’s syndrome simply by watching how your eyes move when trying to look in different directions.
